title: Time, Speed & Distance
shortDescription: Same direction subtracts, opposite direction adds — get the relative-speed rule backwards and every train/boat question after it collapses.
genZNote: Moving toward each other? Speeds team up. Moving the same way? Only the gap between them matters. Mix those two up and the whole question falls apart.

sections.heading: Core Idea
sections.body: Distance = Speed × Time underlies every variant in this topic. The main skill tested is correctly identifying which distance and which relative speed apply to the specific scenario described — trains crossing, boats in a stream, or two bodies moving toward/away from each other.

sections.heading: Relative Speed — the Direction Rule
bullets: Moving TOWARD each other (opposite directions): relative speed = S1 + S2 — they close the gap faster together.
Moving in the SAME direction: relative speed = |S1 − S2| — only the speed GAP matters for one to catch up to the other.

sections.heading: Unit Conversion Shortcut
sections.body: km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5. Memorise 5/18 directly rather than doing the full unit-conversion derivation (×1000/3600) each time.

steps.name: Standard method
steps.explanation: A 120 m train crosses a 180 m platform completely at 20 m/s. Total distance to cover = train length + platform length = 120+180 = 300 m. Time = Distance/Speed = 300/20.
steps.purpose: Crossing a PLATFORM or another train adds both lengths together; crossing a single point (a pole, a standing person) uses ONLY the train's own length.

steps.name: Result
steps.purpose: Confirms the total-distance setup was correct.

sections.heading: Boats & Streams
bullets: Downstream speed = boat speed + stream speed (they add, same as 'moving in the same direction' as the current).
Upstream speed = boat speed − stream speed.
Boat's own speed in still water = (Downstream + Upstream)/2. Stream speed = (Downstream − Upstream)/2 — both reused from the average-of-two-values pattern.

sections.heading: Common Traps
bullets: Forgetting to add the OTHER object's length (platform, bridge, second train) to the distance when a train 'crosses' something — only crossing a single stationary point uses just the train's own length.
Using the SUM of speeds for two bodies moving in the SAME direction (should be the difference), or the DIFFERENCE for bodies moving in opposite directions (should be the sum).
Forgetting to convert units consistently — mixing km/h and m/s in the same calculation without converting first.

sections.heading: Exam Strategy
bullets: Before calculating, identify: (1) which distance actually needs to be covered, and (2) whether the two speeds should add or subtract based on direction.
Convert all speeds to the same unit immediately — this single step prevents most Time-Speed-Distance mistakes.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Distance = Speed × Time; relative speed adds for opposite directions and subtracts for the same direction.
keyFacts: Opposite directions: relative speed = S1+S2. Same direction: relative speed = |S1−S2|.
Crossing a platform/train: total distance = both lengths added. Crossing a pole/point: only the train's own length.
commonConfusion: Same direction subtracts speeds; opposite direction adds them — easy to invert under pressure, always re-check the direction wording.

highYieldFacts: 5/18 (km/h→m/s) and 18/5 (m/s→km/h) should be memorised, not derived each time.
Train crossing a platform/train adds both lengths; crossing a point uses only its own length.
commonTraps: Swapping the add/subtract rule for relative speed based on direction.
Forgetting to add the second object's length when crossing a platform or another train.
